worksheet.title: Spot the Wrong Block
worksheet.subtitle: Compare the plan to the code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find the block with the wrong number.

parts.title: Plan vs code
parts.text: Bit's PLAN says what each step should be. The CODE is what is really there. One block in the code has the WRONG number, so Bit misses the target. Compare the plan to the code to find the wrong block.

parts.title: Plan A (start at 1)
parts.text: The plan is: start at 1, forward 2, forward 1. That lands Bit on 4 (the target).

parts.title: Run Code A
parts.prompt: Run Code A from 1. What number does Bit land on? Did it reach the target (4)?

parts.title: Spot the wrong block
parts.prompt: Compare Code A to the plan. Circle the block that is wrong, and write what it should be.

parts.title: Plan B (start at 5)
parts.text: The plan is: start at 5, back 2, back 1. That lands Bit on 2 (the target).

parts.title: You try — spot it in Code B
parts.prompt: Run Code B from 5. Where does Bit land? Compare to the plan, circle the wrong block, and write what it should be.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To find a bug, compare what the code DOES to what it SHOULD do. The block that does not match the plan is the wrong one.

teacher_guide.title: Spot the Wrong Block
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 2. Spot the Wrong Block — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students locate a bug by comparing a plan (what each step should be) to the code (what is there) and finding the block with the wrong number. Reading existing code against its intended behaviour to find where it goes wrong is the core of C3.2 debugging.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-5 to run the code and the plan and compare where Bit lands.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: run Code A — 'start 1, forward 2 to 3, forward 3 would be 6 but the path ends at 5, so Bit stops on 5. The plan said land on 4 — so there is a bug.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — Code A lands on 5. Exercise 2 — compare to the plan; the last block says forward 3 but the plan says forward 1, so circle forward 3.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — Code B lands on 0; the last block says back 3 but the plan says back 1.
4. Connect: 'Find the bug by checking each block against the plan — the one that does not match is wrong.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Code A: 1 → forward 2 → 3 → forward 3 → stops at 5. Bit lands on 5, not the target 4.
Ex 2 — the wrong block is the last one, forward 3; it should be forward 1 (then 1 → 3 → 4).
Ex 3 — Code B: 5 → back 2 → 3 → back 3 → stops at 0. The wrong block is back 3; it should be back 1 (then 5 → 3 → 2).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: circling a block that matches the plan — have students check each block against the plan, one at a time.
Simplify: read the plan and the code aloud together, pausing at the block that doesn't match.
Extend: ask students to write the corrected Code A and run it to confirm it reaches 4.
Success indicator: the child finds Code A lands on 5 and Code B on 0, and circles forward 3 / back 3 as the wrong blocks with the right fix.
